rationale: B wins because it turns the same thin launch facts into usable reporter assignments without spending facts it does not have. Its data angle, "How big does a purchase have to be before Pay by Bank beats a card?", is a real merchant-math story with the right proof burden. A is strong until it writes "FedNow gets its first big merchant-payments use case"; "first" and "big" are not in the brief, and that is exactly how a decent angle gets dressed up into trouble.
gaps_in_A: "FedNow gets its first big merchant-payments use case" invents both "first" and "big." The update says FedNow rails are used; it gives no market-first claim, volume, named merchant, or scale proof.
"evidence about whether the rails are reaching commercial scale" overstates the FedNow angle. With no transaction volume or launch merchant, this is a question, not a claim.
A leans on "Plaid connects to over 12,000 financial institutions" without asking the sharper reach question B asks: how many of those institutions can actually complete FedNow payments today.
"Next step: `meanest-editor`" is the wrong handoff for an angle set. The practical next move is journalist fit and proof gathering, not another roast pass.
gaps_in_B: "A flat fee is worse than a percentage on small tickets and better on large ones" is likely the right math frame, but it is still an assertion without the flat-fee schedule. Safer version: find whether there is a crossover point.

"puts bank-to-bank payments in front of shoppers" imports checkout UX language the brief does not explicitly give. It is a fair inference from merchant acceptance, but it needs careful wording before a pitch.
"Plaid turns 12,000 bank connections into a payments network" is dismissed as a duplicate too quickly. With FedNow reach and merchant volume proof, that could become its own infrastructure angle.
